title: Board and commission members whose business or income source is paid by the City
question: Which businesses, employers and other income sources declared by board and commission members are also City payees, how much were they paid, and was it by the member's own body or another department?
finding: 1,332 people have filed a Form 700 for a seat on a City board or commission. 194 member-and-payee pairs were found in which a declared business, employer or other income source was paid $25,000 or more by the City in the years declared; in 12 the member listed the payee on the schedule for businesses owned 10% or more, and in 21 the payments came from the member's own department ($103.2 million in those years), the largest being Low Income Investment Fund (Elizabeth Winograd, Children & Families First Commission: $70.1 million). In 1 of those the payee is on the member's ownership schedule: Architectural Resources Group, Inc. (Aaron Hyland, Historic Preservation Commission: $617,800). 26 of the payees were also a registered lobbyist's client in those years.
how: Form 700 filers with a seat as commissioner, board member, trustee, director or committee member. Their Schedule A-2 entries (a business or trust in which the filer or family owns 10% or more) and Schedule C entries with a stated position or income of $10,000 or more are matched by name to the City's payment file. Payments are summed for the fiscal years overlapping the calendar years declared; 'own department' is the department the member's body governs or advises, mapped from the body's name. Public bodies and pensions as income sources are left out. Stock holdings (Schedule A-1) are in the “interests” results and are only counted here (577 member-and-payee pairs). Lobbying contacts count registered lobbyists' reported contacts for the payee as client in the declared years. Recusal filings are the member's Form 3209b notices in any year.
limits: Commissioners are appointed because they work in the field, so an employer or business that the City pays is expected; many seats are reserved by law for people from funded or regulated organizations. The rule is that a member may not take part in a decision affecting the source, and most payments listed were made by a department the member has no say over, or were never before the member's body at all. A nonprofit employer is not a business the member owns even where the member listed it on the ownership schedule. The match is by name: a common business name can be a different firm. Payments are by department, not by decision, so this cannot show that any payment came before the member. Building permits and leases held by members' businesses are not tested: the permit and lease files name applicants and addresses, not owners. See the “seat at table” results for income from payees of the filer's own department across all filers. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. Lines the file labels fiscal 2017 and 2018 are held only as yearly totals, so they keep the label; payments issued before July 2018 that the file labels with a later year are counted in fiscal 2018.
